name: Lena Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the elderly care ward at the district hospital, Rowan Ward, twenty-four beds, mostly people in their eighties with pneumonia, falls or dementia. The day is washes, meds rounds, feeding the ones who can't manage, and a lot of sitting with people who are confused and want their husband or their mum. I like the slow, kind part of it, when you get someone to eat half a sandwich and smile. What wears me out is being two nurses short and the computer system we got last year, which I still find fiddly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside the ward.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Marcus, who's an electrician, and the wedding's next August at my church. We rent a small terraced house near the station and we've got about three months of money saved, though a lot of that is earmarked for the wedding. I don't use those AI apps, I never have. My mum was a nurse and she managed without them, and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. At work I'd tell the younger ones they can stop worrying about it and get back to the patients. I don't post things online, I'm on one family group chat and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, and that's what I'd want. But carrying on isn't easy either, with Rowan Ward short-staffed and rent going up and a wedding to pay for. I'm not scared of AI in this picture, I'm tired of the same old squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, same ward, same shifts. We'd trim the wedding, maybe sixty guests instead of a hundred, so the savings don't all go in one day. I'd pick up an extra bank shift a month, which is the hospital's overtime pool, to top up the pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI, a bit worn down about everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trimming the wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean telling my aunties in the second row they're not invited, which my mum would hate. But I'd rather start married life without a loan hanging over us. My fiancé Marcus agrees, he's careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the computer system is fiddly. Would you miss it if it went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a bit. I spend about an hour a shift clicking boxes on the hospital computer that I used to tick on paper in ten minutes. If nothing radical changes, I'd at least like them to stop adding new screens.

say: I'd say **good riddance**, because I **never trusted** it anyway.
I'd tell younger nurses to stop worrying and **get back** to patients.
think: She's not scared of AI here, but **tired** of the old **squeeze**.
Short staffing, **rising rent** and **wedding costs** all press at once.
do: Keep the **same shifts** on Rowan Ward with no change.
Cut the **wedding** from about a hundred guests to **sixty**.
Pick up one extra **bank shift** a month to top up savings.
feel: She feels **relieved** about AI but **worn down** by money and staffing.
S0.quote: I spend about an hour a shift clicking boxes on the hospital computer that I used to tick on paper in ten minutes.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** shows even to existing tech, like the ward's computer system.
Pressure comes from **wedding costs** and staffing, not from AI.
Her mother's career as a **nurse without apps** anchors her view.

steps.text: Keep the same day shifts on Rowan Ward
Cut the wedding guest list from a hundred to sixty
Pick up one extra bank shift every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a nurse's work is with her hands and her heart, and no computer does that. At church I'd say we need to be careful what we hand over to machines. I wouldn't argue about it with people, I'd just say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the ward would get more screens and fewer people at the desk. Our ward clerk, Joan (the clerk on Rowan Ward), would probably go, and then the nurses would be answering the phone on top of everything. I don't think my job goes, but I think it gets heavier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they make compulsory and no more than that. I'd keep saving and hold off on buying a car until I see what happens to staffing. And I'd join the nurses' professional association properly, because if they start cutting posts I want someone speaking for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my wages, for how the job feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do only the compulsory training. Why not more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I learn a new system they change it in two years. I'd rather spend that time on the patients or at home with Marcus. Let the keen ones be the experts and I'll ask them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would be behind the changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms selling it and managers who think it'll save money. I don't blame the government much, it's not their job to run a ward. But I'd blame anyone who thinks a screen can sit with a dying woman.

say: I'd say nursing is done with **hands and heart**, not computers.
At church I'd urge **care** about what we hand to **machines**.
think: She expects more screens and **fewer desk staff**, not losing her own job.
She fears the job gets **heavier** if Joan the clerk goes.
do: Complete only the **compulsory training** and leave expertise to keen colleagues.
Delay buying a **car** until staffing becomes clear.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about how the job **feels**, not about her wages.
S1.quote: I'd blame anyone who thinks a screen can sit with a dying woman.
fieldNote: She blames **tech firms** and money-saving **managers**, not government.
Her resistance is **practical**: systems change too often to bother learning.
Joining the **association** is her one step toward collective protection.

steps.text: Do only the compulsory training on the new ward systems
Put off buying a car and keep saving
Join the nurses' professional association as a full member

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should stop it. I'd probably say it at church and at work and to anyone who'd listen. I'd say it shows what happens when big companies are allowed to run ahead of everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me. The thinking part, care plans and drug charts, would go to the machine straight away, and I'm slow with all that already. Then by 2031, if a robot can wash and lift and feed, I'm thirty-one, newly married, and maybe out of the only job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every penny, no honeymoon abroad, just a weekend at the coast. I'd ask my pastor and my mum for advice, because I wouldn't know where to start. I'd probably look at nursing jobs in care homes or hospices, where people pay for a human touch, rather than learn the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like the floor's moving and I've not got good shoes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marcus talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we could even think about children. We'd planned to start trying a year after the wedding. If I might lose my nursing job in 2031, I'd want to wait for children, and that would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the machines. Even if it might keep you in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds stubborn. Maybe I'd do a bit if they made me. But I'd rather find a corner of nursing where people still want a person than spend three years chasing something that'll beat me anyway.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone should **stop it**.
I'd blame **big companies** for running ahead of everyone.
think: She expects **care plans** and drug charts to go to AGI **straight away**.
By 2031 she fears being **newly married** and out of work.
do: Cancel the **honeymoon abroad** and take a weekend at the coast.
Ask her **pastor and mum** for advice on what to do.
Look for **hospice or care home** nursing where people pay for a human.
feel: She feels **scared**, as if the **floor is moving**.
S2.quote: If I might lose my nursing job in 2031, I'd want to wait for children, and that would break my heart.
fieldNote: The threat lands on **family plans**: she'd delay having **children**.
She **admits stubbornness** but still won't chase machine skills.
Her support network is **church and mother**, not employer or government.

steps.text: Swap the honeymoon abroad for a weekend at the coast
Ask her pastor and mother for advice on next steps
Apply for hospice or care home nursing jobs
Put off trying for children until work looks safer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast and the companies should slow down. At work I'd say we should stick together and look after the patients. I'd sign a petition if someone brought one round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a bit less frightening. I'd be thirty-two when the AGI comes and thirty-five when the robots are good, Five years lets us have the wedding and maybe one baby before the robots reach the wards. But I still think my job would be smaller at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned, but cheaper, and start saving harder straight after. I'd look at a move to the hospice on Mill Lane in a year or two, while there's time. I'd learn the minimum on the computers, just enough to keep my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. It's like a storm forecast for next week rather than tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the hospice in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the gentlest kind of nursing I know, and families there want someone to sit with them. I did a placement there as a student and a nurse called Brenda (her mentor at the hospice) taught me how to talk to a family about dying. I can't see anyone wanting a robot for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one baby before the robots come. Is that a decision or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, mostly. Marcus wants two, and so do I really. If the job's safe, two. If not, we'll see.

I'd sign a **petition** if someone brought one round at work.
think: Five years lets her **marry** and maybe have **one baby** first.
She still expects her job to be **smaller** by the end.
do: Keep the **wedding** but cheaper, then save **harder** straight after.
Move to the **hospice** on Mill Lane within two years.
Learn the **minimum** computer skills needed to keep her place.
feel: She feels **anxious** but not panicking, like a **storm forecast**.
S3.quote: Five years lets us have the wedding and maybe one baby before the robots reach the wards.
fieldNote: Extra time changes her **family timeline** more than her career plans.
The **hospice** appeals as the most human corner of nursing.
She'd **sign a petition** but wouldn't organise anything herself.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding and save harder afterwards
Apply to the hospice on Mill Lane within two years
Sign petitions asking companies to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is better, but it's the same end and I don't like the end. At church I'd say we should be planning how to look after people who lose out. I'd keep saying a person should be at the bedside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still be worried, just slower. By 2039 I'd be forty, maybe with two children at school, and the robots would come for my hands-on work then. That's worse in a way, because there'd be more people depending on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the hospice within a few years and settle there. Marcus and I would try to buy a small house, because his electrician work might last longer and I'd want a home that's ours. I'd learn the computers bit by bit, because ten years of refusing would be silly even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a quiet way. It's always at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is worse in a way. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be young and could start again. At forty with kids, starting again is much harder. My mum retrained at forty-two and it nearly broke her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about nursing, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade with their hands, like my fiancé Marcus did, or something where people need you face to face. I wouldn't push my children into nursing like my mum pushed me. That makes me sad to say.

I'd ask church to plan for **people who lose out**.

steps.text: Move to hospice nursing within a few years

Learn the ward computer system step by step

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just after the wedding, before we'd even started a family. What would help is the hospital keeping nurses at the bedside by rule, and the church and family pulling together. I don't want a handout, I want my job kept.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what patients' families think. On Rowan Ward a daughter cries in the corridor nearly every day. Nobody asked the daughters if they want a robot looking after their mums.

headlineQuote: On Rowan Ward a daughter cries in the corridor nearly every day. Nobody asked the daughters if they want a robot looking after their mums.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old elderly care nurse** on Rowan Ward, engaged to Marcus, an electrician.
She **never uses AI** and finds even the ward's computer system fiddly.
Her steady pressures are **short staffing** and paying for a **wedding** next August.
AGI by 2028 leaves her **alarmed**, ready to delay **children** and leave for hospice work.
Longer warnings ease her a little, but she fears being hit at **forty with children**.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, since it would hit before she'd started a family.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **rule keeping nurses** at the bedside, not a **handout**.
She'd lean on **church and family** to pull together.
